primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- a first-year assessment of Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., organized around the reform program CJP calls "The Davide Watch" and its core values IIEE for the bench and EP for the bar.

The spiritual origin CJP attributes to the Davide program: the 2 Maccabees 10 passage on the purification of temple and city that Davide read on the morning he was sworn in, and his consequent conviction that his mission is to cleanse the judicial stables and to call for metanoia.

A systematic inventory of concrete first-year measures under each value -- fiscal and political independence, integrity and transparency, excellence through education and speedy justice, and effectiveness through reorganization and judicial dialogs -- plus the parallel program for a reformed bar.

An essay on Davide's juridical thought and decision-writing style, offering four impressions (pro-environment, a stickler for the rule of law, conventional yet capable of innovation, and deeply spiritual) while conceding the peril of labeling any jurist's school of jurisprudence.
The unifying thesis of the book's title: that the Chief Justice's whole program and philosophy are sewn together by the credo Leadership by Example, itself the gospel Jesus taught his disciples.
sub_topics: Davide's elevation on November 30, 1998 acclaimed as President Estrada's best first-year appointment, conceded even by the critic Jovito R. Salonga and applauded by the Philippine Daily Inquirer, the Philippine Star and the Manila Bulletin.

Pulse Asia surveys of June and September 1999 showing the Supreme Court topping approval ratings among government agencies, tempered by CJP's caveat that the Court does not thrive in a popularity contest but must enjoy residual public respect so its decisions are obeyed.
The unconventional swearing-in without a written appointment during the Bonifacio Day celebrations, the day after CJ Narvasa vacated the post.

Davide's morning habit of prayer and of cutting the Bible at random, and the 2 Maccabees 10 passage on the purification of the temple that he read on November 30, 1998, confirmed for him by the next day's Responsorial Psalm.

His Knights of Columbus speech of January 10, 1999 on metanoia -- the change of heart that must precede any institutional or societal change -- and CJP's forecast that he will demand higher ethical values expressed in the natural law.
The secular "opportunity for greatness" open to every Chief Justice, with the examples of Teehankee and Fernan at home and of John Marshall and Earl Warren in the United States.

The Davide Watch reproduced in full: the policy statement, the vision of an independent, effective and efficient judiciary and an ethical, accessible legal profession, and the mission items on independence, effectiveness and efficiency, public trust and confidence, and the legal profession.

CJP's observation that the Chief Justice of the Philippines is comparatively more powerful than counterparts abroad, because the judiciary may nullify grave abuse of discretion by any branch and supervises the lower courts and the bar.
The SC-UNDP-funded development plan and the forthcoming Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary headed by Justice Bellosillo, whose core is Sustainable Human Development.

Independence in practice: the judiciary's budget at only 1.12 percent of the national budget, salaries pegged to the Salary Standardization Law, and Davide's success in convincing Congress to grant lump-sum appropriations from the year 2000.

Independence from partisan politics through the Judicial and Bar Council -- regular interviews of nominees, full-time members travelling to far-flung provinces, and Resolution JBC-007 directing wide publicity of nominations -- plus resolutions granting benefits to judicial personnel.

Integrity: Davide's unquestioned personal probity, his call for transparency without betraying confidential aspects of the judicial process, and the creation of the Committee on Public Information (chaired by CJP) and a Public Information Office under Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr.

Judicial cleansing through hastened administrative cases, listed one by one -- among them Astih, Villanueva, Esteban, Santos, Dames, Lustre, Yaneza, Calderon, Escano, Lledo, Blanca, Rivota and Zoleta -- ending in dismissals, forfeitures, suspensions and fines.

Excellence: completing PHILJA's facilities under Justice Melencio-Herrera, tapping the World Bank, JICA and private foundations, exchange and computerization programs, video-conferencing, and the Court's new web page.

Speedy justice: St. Martin Funeral Home v. NLRC, Fabian v. Ombudsman and National Federation of Labor v. Laguesma redirecting cases to the Court of Appeals, resolutions dismissing misfiled petitions, limits on extensions for the Solicitor General, the abolition of rejoinders, and the transfer of family-court cases to the regional trial courts.

Effectiveness and efficiency: reorganization of Divisions and committees, and the first-ever judicial dialogs in every region, including the Cagayan de Oro sortie of August 20, 1999 that CJP joined, after which the judges wrote an "Article of Faith" thanking the Chief for coming down from his pedestal of power.

A dozen administrative circulars on the dignity of courts, working and session hours, restraint in issuing TROs, prompt action on letters, banning smoking, uniforms and qualifications for judicial office.

A reformed bar: Davide's IBP House of Delegates and Cebu speeches on highly informed and exceptionally moral lawyers who honor every word of the Lawyer's Oath, the Mandatory Continuing Legal Education program before the Vitug Committee, and the IBP's accelerated discipline cases and the Court's disbarment decisions.

The Japanese and Korean models of limiting bar entry -- three percent and two percent passing rates plus a mandatory one-and-a-half-year training -- which impressed Davide at the Lawasia conference in Seoul.

The essay on Davide's juridical thought: the difficulty Justice Quiason noted in categorizing a jurist, Davide's own refusal to advocate any school, CJP's disagreement with that refusal, and the new world order of globalization and technology awaiting the Court.
His decision-writing style -- exhaustive, clear, unequivocal, plain enough for lay readers, free of obiters and flourish, always leaving quotable doctrine.

Four impressions: pro-environment (Oposa v. Factoran and Tano v. Socrates); a stickler for the rule of law (People v. Quijada and Regala v. Sandiganbayan); conventional yet capable of innovation (the PIRMA and Santiago v. Comelec ruling on RA 6735, which CJP researched and opposed in dissent); and deeply spiritual.

Epilogue: the pledge before the Kilosbayan Forum to spare no effort in leading the judiciary by example, the contrast with leaders who lord it over their followers, and the passage from Mark in which Jesus tells his disciples that whoever wishes to be great must be servant of all.

stances.claim: Davide's first year justifies calling his elevation an auspicious beginning, because the acclaim came even from the President's harshest critics and because the Court topped nationwide approval ratings.
stances.rhetorical_move: corroboration from hostile witnesses -- a critic's concession and independent survey data offered before any of CJP's own praise

stances.claim: Public approval is not the measure of the Court's work, since its members decide on reasoned arguments and precedent rather than momentary sentiment; yet the Court must retain enough residual public respect that its decisions are obeyed even when the majority disagrees.
stances.rhetorical_move: concession-and-qualification: rejecting popularity as a test while preserving public confidence as a condition of institutional survival

stances.claim: To preserve judicial independence the Constitution should have fixed a percentage of the annual national budget for the judiciary, disbursed by the Supreme Court subject only to audit; failing that, Davide's lump-sum appropriation was the next best thing.
stances.rhetorical_move: ideal-versus-attainable framing -- stating the constitutional remedy he would prefer, then crediting the practical second best

stances.claim: Every leader must have a well-defined philosophy, so CJP respectfully disagrees with Davide's position that jurists have neither need nor reason to advocate one school of thought.
stances.rhetorical_move: open disagreement with the subject of his own tribute, quoted fairly and then answered in one sentence

stances.claim: The theory that RA 6735 was an "insufficient law" was novel and unsupported by credible authority here or abroad, and should not have diminished the people's right to initiative, which institutionalized people power.
stances.rhetorical_move: research-backed dissent recalled: reporting his own failed search for authority and his losing dissent while still crediting Davide's capacity to innovate

stances.claim: The Chief Justice of the Philippines is comparatively more powerful than his counterparts elsewhere, including the United States, because of the power to nullify grave abuse of discretion by any branch and the Court's supervision of the lower courts and the bar.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative institutional argument stated in two numbered points

notable_anecdotes: Davide's account of waking at 3:30 a.m. on November 30, 1998, praying and cutting the New American Bible, which opened on 2 Maccabees 10, "Purification of Temple and City" -- a title that struck him and that he read and reread.
The Responsorial Psalm of the following day, "Justice shall flourish in His time, and the fullness of peace forever," which he took as confirmation of the message to purify the temple.
The unconventional swearing-in without any written appointment during the Bonifacio Day celebrations, the day after Chief Justice Narvasa vacated the post.

The media courtship of the new Chief -- a dinner in his honor at the Philippine Daily Inquirer headquarters on December 14, 1998 and a private lunch hosted by Max V. Soliven at Dr. Preciosa S. Soliven's La Dolce Fontana.

The doubts inside the Court when the Committee on Public Information was proposed -- why should the Court need public relations? -- and CJP's answer that its work is simply to tell the whole truth about the Court.

The Cagayan de Oro sortie of August 20, 1999: landing at 6:30 a.m., four hours with about 800 court personnel in a hotel conference hall, then an afternoon with some 50 trial judges, after which the judges wrote an "Article of Faith" saying how deeply touched they were that the highest official had come down from his pedestal of power.

CJP's own one-sentence Filipino description of Davide at a Court function on October 22, 1997 as the epitome of the Filipino jurist -- makabayan, maginoo, marangal, matapang, masipag, mapagkakatiwalaan.
The recollection of losing the PIRMA case: after researching long and hard without finding authority for the "insufficient law" theory, CJP had to be content with writing a dissent.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' assessed the first year of Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., whose elevation on November 30, 1998 Justice Panganiban reported as universally acclaimed -- even by the President's critics, and reflected in Pulse Asia surveys showing the Supreme Court topping approval ratings, though he cautioned that the Court does not thrive on popularity but must keep enough residual public respect for its decisions to be obeyed. He traced the program's origin to Davide's habit of cutting the Bible at random: on the morning of his oath-taking it opened on 2 Maccabees 10, "Purification of Temple and City," which Davide read as a commission to cleanse the judicial stables and, in his Knights of Columbus speech, as a call to metanoia before any institutional change. CJP then reproduced "The Davide Watch" in full -- its policy statement, its vision of a judiciary independent, effective, efficient and worthy of public trust and of a legal profession that is ethical and accessible, and its mission items -- and summarized its core values as IIEE for the bench and EP for the bar, noting the SC-UNDP-funded Blueprint of Action then forthcoming under Justice Bellosillo. He inventoried the first-year measures: lump-sum appropriations won from Congress against a judiciary budget of only 1.12 percent of the national total; a more transparent Judicial and Bar Council; the new Committee on Public Information he was asked to chair and a Public Information Office under Atty. Khan; a long list of administrative cases ending in dismissals and forfeitures; PHILJA's strengthening, computerization and the Court's new web page; rulings such as St. Martin Funeral Home and Fabian that redirected appeals to the Court of Appeals; reorganized Divisions; the first regional judicial dialogs, including the Cagayan de Oro sortie he joined; and a reform program for the bar built on mandatory continuing legal education and accelerated discipline. He closed with an essay on Davide's decision-writing and juridical thought -- pro-environment in Oposa and Tano, a stickler for the rule of law in Quijada and Regala, conventional yet capable of the innovation CJP had opposed in the PIRMA case, and deeply spiritual -- all sewn together, he argued, by the credo Leadership by Example, which he traced to the Gospel of Mark.
